items.stem: Which of the following best describes "price inelastic supply"?
options: The ease with which resources can be moved from one use to another; greater mobility makes supply more elastic
Supply for which 0 < PES < 1, so quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price
The ability of a firm to increase output using existing equipment and workers that are not fully used, which makes supply more elastic
Supply for which PES > 1, so quantity supplied changes by a larger percentage than price
items.answer: Supply for which 0 < PES < 1, so quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price
items.markingKey: B. "price inelastic supply" is supply for which 0 < PES < 1, so quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price.

items.stem: Briefly explain why PES matters for how a market responds to an increase in demand.
items.answer: If supply is elastic, firms expand output easily, so an increase in demand mainly raises quantity with a small price rise; if supply is inelastic, the same increase in demand mainly raises price.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If supply is elastic, firms expand output easily, so an increase in demand mainly raises quantity with a small price rise; if supply is inelastic, the same increase in demand mainly raises price. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that a steep supply curve through the origin is inelastic. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1 regardless of its slope.
items.markingKey: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1 regardless of its slope. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mei writes: "PES of 0.5 means quantity supplied falls when price rises." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: PES is positive: quantity supplied rises, but by only half the percentage change in price.
items.markingKey: PES is positive: quantity supplied rises, but by only half the percentage change in price. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which hotel rooms in Edinburgh during the August festival season shows price inelastic supply.
items.answer: Room prices rise sharply every August as visitors arrive for the festivals, while the number of rooms in the city stays the same. The stock of rooms is fixed in the short run, so higher demand mainly raised prices rather than quantity supplied.
items.markingKey: Context (Room prices rise sharply every August as visitors arrive for the festivals, while the number of rooms in the city stays the same.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The stock of rooms is fixed in the short run, so higher demand mainly raised prices rather than quantity supplied. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to price inelastic supply.

items.stem: Explain, using diagrams, the effect of an increase in demand on price and quantity when supply is (i) perfectly inelastic, (ii) price inelastic and (iii) price elastic.
items.answer: (i) vertical S: only price rises; (ii) steep S: large price rise, small quantity rise; (iii) flat S: small price rise, large quantity rise. Each diagram shows D1 to D2.
items.markingKey: (i) vertical S: only price rises; (ii) steep S: large price rise, small quantity rise; (iii) flat S: small price rise, large quantity rise. Each diagram shows D1 to D2.

items.stem: Define the term "price inelastic supply".
items.answer: Supply for which 0 < PES < 1, so quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: supply for which 0 < PES < 1, so quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "perfectly elastic supply".
items.answer: Supply for which PES is infinite, shown by a horizontal supply curve: firms will supply any quantity at a given price
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: supply for which PES is infinite, shown by a horizontal supply curve: firms will supply any quantity at a given price. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between PES and PED.
items.answer: PED measures consumers' responsiveness to price (normally negative); PES measures producers' responsiveness to price (normally positive).
items.markingKey: PED measures consumers' responsiveness to price (normally negative); PES measures producers' responsiveness to price (normally positive). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a linear supply curve that cuts the quantity axis is price inelastic.
items.answer: Such a line has a positive quantity at zero price, so a given percentage change in price produces a smaller percentage change in quantity; PES = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) < 1 at every point.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Such a line has a positive quantity at zero price, so a given percentage change in price produces a smaller percentage change in quantity; PES = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) < 1 at every point. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: When the price received by copper mines in Chile changed from $50 to $70, quantity supplied changed from 10,000 to 18,000 tonnes per month. Calculate the PES.
items.answer: PES = 2 (price elastic)

items.stem: The price of strawberries in Lisbon rose by 25% and the quantity supplied to the market rose by 5% within a week. Calculate PES and comment.
items.answer: PES = 5/25 = 0.2: very inelastic – farmers cannot quickly grow more strawberries in a week.
items.markingKey: PES = 5/25 = 0.2: very inelastic – farmers cannot quickly grow more strawberries in a week.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how the price elasticity of supply affects the impact of an increase in demand on price and quantity, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Two diagrams: same rightward demand shift D1 to D2. With inelastic (steep) supply, price rises a lot (P1 to P2) and quantity a little; with elastic (flat) supply, price rises little and quantity a lot. Label PES < 1 and PES > 1.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two diagrams: same rightward demand shift D1 to D2. With inelastic (steep) supply, price rises a lot (P1 to P2) and quantity a little; with elastic (flat) supply, price rises little and quantity a lot. Label PES < 1 and PES > 1. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

When the average price of a three-bedroom house in Auckland rose by 20% between 2020 and 2021, the number of new homes completed rose by only 4%. Builders reported shortages of land with planning permission and of skilled workers.
— Extract based on housing-market reporting

Calculate the PES for new homes and use the extract to explain the value.
items.answer: PES = 4/20 = 0.2: inelastic; shortages of land with planning permission and skilled labour, and long construction times, limit how fast supply can respond.
items.markingKey: PES = 4/20 = 0.2: inelastic; shortages of land with planning permission and skilled labour, and long construction times, limit how fast supply can respond. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that increasing the price elasticity of supply is the best way to reduce price volatility in housing markets.
items.answer: Raising PES is important for long-run affordability, but in the short run demand-side policies are often needed as well.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: more elastic supply means demand shocks raise quantity rather than price; planning reform and land release can raise PES. Arguments against: housing supply is limited by land and construction time; demand-side policies (interest rates, taxes on investors) can be quicker; building more may conflict with environmental goals. Judgement: Raising PES is important for long-run affordability, but in the short run demand-side policies are often needed as well. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mobility of factors of production"?
options: Supply for which PES = 1; any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1
Supply for which PES > 1, so quantity supplied changes by a larger percentage than price
The ease with which resources can be moved from one use to another; greater mobility makes supply more elastic
Supply for which 0 < PES < 1, so quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price
items.answer: The ease with which resources can be moved from one use to another; greater mobility makes supply more elastic
items.markingKey: C. "mobility of factors of production" is the ease with which resources can be moved from one use to another; greater mobility makes supply more elastic.

items.stem: Explain why spare capacity makes supply more price elastic.
items.answer: A firm with idle machinery and workers can increase output quickly and without a large rise in costs when price rises, so quantity supplied responds strongly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A firm with idle machinery and workers can increase output quickly and without a large rise in costs when price rises, so quantity supplied responds strongly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Felix writes: "Supply is always more elastic for expensive goods." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: PES depends on time, spare capacity, stocks and factor mobility, not on whether a good is expensive.
items.markingKey: PES depends on time, spare capacity, stocks and factor mobility, not on whether a good is expensive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the supply of electricity from gas-fired power stations is more price elastic than from nuclear power stations.
items.answer: Gas plants can be switched on and off quickly to raise output when prices rise; nuclear stations run at a constant level and cannot easily increase output, so their supply is inelastic.
items.markingKey: Gas plants can be switched on and off quickly to raise output when prices rise; nuclear stations run at a constant level and cannot easily increase output, so their supply is inelastic.

items.stem: The price of face masks in Seoul rose by 50% from an initial quantity supplied of 2,000 units. Quantity supplied was 2400 after one week, 2500 after six months and 3200 after three years. Calculate PES for each period and explain the pattern.
items.markingKey: %ΔQs each period / 50%: 0.4, 0.5, 1.2 [2]; supply becomes more elastic over time as firms add capacity, workers and new firms enter [2].

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Firms should always hold large stocks so that their supply is price elastic.
items.answer: Holding stocks increases PES, but the optimal level balances responsiveness against storage and financing costs.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stocks allow firms to respond quickly to price rises and gain revenue; reduces the risk of shortages. Arguments against: storage costs, waste and obsolescence; ties up working capital; perishable goods cannot be stored. Supported judgement: Holding stocks increases PES, but the optimal level balances responsiveness against storage and financing costs.

items.stem: In which time period is supply most price elastic?
options: It is the same in every period
The short run
The long run
The momentary period
items.answer: The long run
items.markingKey: C. In the long run all factors can change and new firms can enter.

items.stem: Explain why supply becomes more elastic over time.
items.answer: In the short run some factors are fixed and firms can only use existing capacity; in the long run they can build new capacity, hire and train workers and new firms can enter.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In the short run some factors are fixed and firms can only use existing capacity; in the long run they can build new capacity, hire and train workers and new firms can enter. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the mobility of factors of production affects PES.
items.answer: If labour and capital can easily switch between uses (e.g. a factory switching from one garment to another), firms can quickly increase output of the good whose price rises, making supply elastic.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If labour and capital can easily switch between uses (e.g. a factory switching from one garment to another), firms can quickly increase output of the good whose price rises, making supply elastic. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between perishable goods and goods that can be stored.
items.answer: Storable goods can be released from stocks when price rises, so supply is more elastic; perishable goods cannot be stored, so supply is more inelastic.
items.markingKey: Storable goods can be released from stocks when price rises, so supply is more elastic; perishable goods cannot be stored, so supply is more inelastic. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

After a viral social-media trend in 2023, the price of a particular brand of insulated water bottle doubled on resale sites. The manufacturer said it could not raise output for several months because its factories in China were already running 24 hours a day and new moulds took time to make.
— Extract based on news reporting

Using the extract, explain why the supply of the bottles was price inelastic in the short run.
items.answer: The factories had no spare capacity (already at full use) and new equipment takes time to produce, so quantity supplied could not respond quickly to the higher price: PES was low in the short run.
items.markingKey: The factories had no spare capacity (already at full use) and new equipment takes time to produce, so quantity supplied could not respond quickly to the higher price: PES was low in the short run. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using the shortage of semiconductors in 2021 as an example, explain time and capacity as determinants of PES.
items.answer: Car makers faced chip shortages for over a year because building a new fabrication plant takes 2-3 years and costs over $10 billion. Supply was inelastic in the short run because capacity was fully used and new plants take years to build.
items.markingKey: Context (Car makers faced chip shortages for over a year because building a new fabrication plant takes 2-3 years and costs over $10 billion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Supply was inelastic in the short run because capacity was fully used and new plants take years to build. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to time and capacity as determinants of PES.

items.stem: Low PES combined with low PED in commodity markets results in which of the following?
options: Large price fluctuations when demand or supply shifts
Perfectly elastic demand
Stable prices
Constant revenues for producers
items.answer: Large price fluctuations when demand or supply shifts
items.markingKey: A. Steep curves mean small shifts cause large price changes.

items.stem: Distinguish between price volatility and a long-term price trend.
items.answer: Volatility refers to short-term fluctuations up and down; a trend is the direction of prices over many years.
items.markingKey: Volatility refers to short-term fluctuations up and down; a trend is the direction of prices over many years. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the supply of agricultural products is price inelastic in the short run.
items.answer: Crops and livestock take time to grow; once planted, output is fixed until harvest, land is limited and weather affects yields, so farmers cannot respond quickly to price changes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Crops and livestock take time to grow; once planted, output is fixed until harvest, land is limited and weather affects yields, so farmers cannot respond quickly to price changes. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that Farmers can quickly increase supply when prices rise because land is always available. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Land is limited and crops take time to grow, so supply is inelastic in the short run.
items.markingKey: Land is limited and crops take time to grow, so supply is inelastic in the short run. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate why the prices of primary commodities are more volatile than the prices of manufactured goods, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Two diagrams. Commodity: steep (inelastic) demand and supply; a supply shift (e.g. bad harvest) causes a large price change. Manufactured good: flatter (elastic) supply; the same demand or supply shift causes a smaller price change and a larger quantity change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two diagrams. Commodity: steep (inelastic) demand and supply; a supply shift (e.g. bad harvest) causes a large price change. Manufactured good: flatter (elastic) supply; the same demand or supply shift causes a smaller price change and a larger quantity change. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Buffer stock schemes are the best way to stabilise primary commodity prices.
items.answer: Buffer stocks can reduce short-term volatility for storable goods but have often failed because of cost and mis-set prices; diversification and insurance may be better long-term solutions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: buying in surplus years and selling in shortage years reduces volatility; stabilises farmers' incomes. Arguments against: expensive storage and administration; difficult to set the right target price; schemes such as the International Tin Agreement collapsed in 1985; perishable goods cannot be stored. Supported judgement: Buffer stocks can reduce short-term volatility for storable goods but have often failed because of cost and mis-set prices; diversification and insurance may be better long-term solutions.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why PES for coffee is low?
options: Coffee is a necessity
Coffee is produced in many countries
Coffee plants take three to four years to start producing
Demand for coffee is inelastic
items.answer: Coffee plants take three to four years to start producing
items.markingKey: C. Long gestation periods prevent a quick supply response.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Because commodity prices are volatile, PES for commodities must be high." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Volatility results from low (inelastic) PES and PED: small shifts in curves cause large price changes.
items.markingKey: Volatility results from low (inelastic) PES and PED: small shifts in curves cause large price changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how low PES contributes to income instability for commodity-exporting countries.
items.answer: Low PES (and PED) mean shocks cause large price swings; because export revenues depend on prices, incomes, government revenue and the exchange rate fluctuate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Low PES (and PED) mean shocks cause large price swings; because export revenues depend on prices, incomes, government revenue and the exchange rate fluctuate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Because commodity prices are volatile, PES for commodities must be high." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Volatility results from low (inelastic) PES and PED: small shifts in curves cause large price changes.
items.markingKey: Volatility results from low (inelastic) PES and PED: small shifts in curves cause large price changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Over one year the price of palm oil rose by 20% and the quantity supplied rose by 4%. Over the same year the price of smartphone cases rose by 20% and the quantity supplied rose by 50%. Calculate the PES for each product and explain the difference.
items.answer: palm oil: PES = 0.2; smartphone cases: PES = 2.5
items.markingKey: palm oil: 4/20 = 0.2 [1]; smartphone cases: 50/20 = 2.5 [1]; commodity supply inelastic because of gestation periods/fixed land or long mine lead times, manufacturing elastic because of spare capacity, stocks and factor mobility [2].

items.stem: A student claims that because commodity prices are volatile, PES for commodities must be high. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Volatility results from low (inelastic) PES and PED: small shifts in curves cause large price changes.
items.markingKey: Volatility results from low (inelastic) PES and PED: small shifts in curves cause large price changes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the 2014-2016 collapse in oil prices shows low PES and price volatility in primary commodity markets.
items.answer: Oil prices fell from over $100 to under $30 a barrel as US shale output grew and OPEC did not cut production. With inelastic short-run demand and supply, rising supply caused a dramatic fall in price.
items.markingKey: Context (Oil prices fell from over $100 to under $30 a barrel as US shale output grew and OPEC did not cut production.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: With inelastic short-run demand and supply, rising supply caused a dramatic fall in price. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to low PES and price volatility in primary commodity markets.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "unit elastic supply".
items.answer: Supply for which PES = 1; any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: supply for which PES = 1; any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "stocks (inventories)".
items.answer: Goods held in storage that can be released onto the market quickly, increasing the elasticity of supply
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: goods held in storage that can be released onto the market quickly, increasing the elasticity of supply. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "manufactured product".
items.answer: A good produced in the secondary sector by processing raw materials, often in factories
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a good produced in the secondary sector by processing raw materials, often in factories. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between perfectly inelastic supply and perfectly elastic supply.
items.answer: Perfectly elastic supply is horizontal: any quantity at the given price; perfectly inelastic supply is vertical: quantity is fixed whatever the price.
items.markingKey: Perfectly elastic supply is horizontal: any quantity at the given price; perfectly inelastic supply is vertical: quantity is fixed whatever the price. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "If a factory is working at full capacity, its supply is perfectly elastic." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: At full capacity, output cannot rise easily, so supply is inelastic in the short run.
items.markingKey: At full capacity, output cannot rise easily, so supply is inelastic in the short run. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Farmers can quickly increase supply when prices rise because land is always available." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Land is limited and crops take time to grow, so supply is inelastic in the short run.
items.markingKey: Land is limited and crops take time to grow, so supply is inelastic in the short run. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between PED and PES.
items.answer: PED measures consumers' responsiveness to price (normally negative); PES measures producers' responsiveness to price (normally positive).
items.markingKey: PED measures consumers' responsiveness to price (normally negative); PES measures producers' responsiveness to price (normally positive). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the long run (for PES) and the short run.
items.answer: In the short run at least one factor is fixed so supply is relatively inelastic; in the long run all factors can change and firms can enter or leave, so supply is more elastic.
items.markingKey: In the short run at least one factor is fixed so supply is relatively inelastic; in the long run all factors can change and firms can enter or leave, so supply is more elastic. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between PES for primary commodities and PES for manufactured products.
items.answer: Commodities have low PES because of growing times, fixed land and long investment lead times; manufactured goods have higher PES because factories can use spare capacity, stocks and mobile factors to raise output quickly.
items.markingKey: Commodities have low PES because of growing times, fixed land and long investment lead times; manufactured goods have higher PES because factories can use spare capacity, stocks and mobile factors to raise output quickly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Maya writes: "A steep supply curve through the origin is inelastic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1 regardless of its slope.
items.markingKey: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1 regardless of its slope. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: PES depends on time, spare capacity, stocks and factor mobility, not on whether a good is expensive.
items.markingKey: PES depends on time, spare capacity, stocks and factor mobility, not on whether a good is expensive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the world price of cocoa rose to over $10,000 per tonne in 2024 after poor harvests in West Africa.
items.answer: Cocoa supply is price inelastic (new trees take years to mature, disease and weather limit output) and demand is inelastic, so a leftward supply shift caused a very large price rise.
items.markingKey: Cocoa supply is price inelastic (new trees take years to mature, disease and weather limit output) and demand is inelastic, so a leftward supply shift caused a very large price rise.

items.stem: With reference to hotel rooms in Edinburgh during the August festival season, explain how it illustrates price inelastic supply.

items.stem: Using the global response to demand for Covid-19 vaccines in 2021 as an example, explain how PES increases over time.
items.answer: Vaccine output was initially limited, but within a year manufacturers had converted and built plants and supplied billions of doses. Supply was very inelastic in the first months but became much more elastic as new capacity was built and factors were moved into production.

items.stem: Briefly describe the 2014-2016 collapse in oil prices and explain what it reveals about low PES and price volatility in primary commodity markets.
items.answer: Oil prices fell from over $100 to under $30 a barrel as US shale output grew and OPEC did not cut production. With inelastic short-run demand and supply, rising supply caused a dramatic fall in price.

items.stem: A sudden rise in demand increases the price of bicycles. Explain how the PES of bicycles might differ in the momentary period, the short run and the long run.
items.answer: Momentary: only existing stock – very inelastic; short run: overtime, use of spare capacity – more elastic; long run: new factories, new firms – elastic. Diagram with three supply curves pivoting through the original equilibrium.
items.markingKey: Momentary: only existing stock – very inelastic; short run: overtime, use of spare capacity – more elastic; long run: new factories, new firms – elastic. Diagram with three supply curves pivoting through the original equilibrium.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that countries that depend on primary commodity exports should diversify into manufacturing.
items.answer: Diversification reduces risk and supports development, but it should build on existing strengths and be pursued gradually.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reduces exposure to volatile commodity prices; manufacturing has higher YED and PES; creates more jobs and skills. Arguments against: comparative advantage may lie in commodities; diversification takes time and investment; some commodities have strong future demand (energy transition minerals). Judgement: Diversification reduces risk and supports development, but it should build on existing strengths and be pursued gradually. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that increasing the price elasticity of supply is the best way to reduce price volatility in housing markets.
items.answer: Raising PES is important for long-run affordability, but in the short run demand-side policies are often needed as well.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: more elastic supply means demand shocks raise quantity rather than price; planning reform and land release can raise PES. Arguments against: housing supply is limited by land and construction time; demand-side policies (interest rates, taxes on investors) can be quicker; building more may conflict with environmental goals. Judgement: Raising PES is important for long-run affordability, but in the short run demand-side policies are often needed as well. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that time is the most important determinant of the price elasticity of supply.
items.answer: Time is usually the most important determinant because it governs the ability to change all inputs, but stocks and spare capacity determine short-run responses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: in the long run new capacity and firms enter (all goods); explains why commodity supply responds slowly. Arguments against: spare capacity allows a quick response even in the short run; stocks and storability matter for many goods; some supplies are fixed whatever the time (land, rare art). Judgement: Time is usually the most important determinant because it governs the ability to change all inputs, but stocks and spare capacity determine short-run responses. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "price elasticity of supply (PES)".
items.answer: A measure of the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's price, calculated as %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a measure of the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's price, calculated as %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "time period (as a determinant of PES)".

items.stem: "A steep supply curve through the origin is inelastic." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1 regardless of its slope.
items.markingKey: Any straight-line supply curve through the origin has PES = 1 regardless of its slope. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between goods that can be stored and perishable goods.
items.answer: Storable goods can be released from stocks when price rises, so supply is more elastic; perishable goods cannot be stored, so supply is more inelastic.
items.markingKey: Storable goods can be released from stocks when price rises, so supply is more elastic; perishable goods cannot be stored, so supply is more inelastic. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Farmers can quickly increase supply when prices rise because land is always available." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Land is limited and crops take time to grow, so supply is inelastic in the short run.
items.markingKey: Land is limited and crops take time to grow, so supply is inelastic in the short run. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between perfectly elastic supply and perfectly inelastic supply.
items.answer: Perfectly elastic supply is horizontal: any quantity at the given price; perfectly inelastic supply is vertical: quantity is fixed whatever the price.
items.markingKey: Perfectly elastic supply is horizontal: any quantity at the given price; perfectly inelastic supply is vertical: quantity is fixed whatever the price. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why mining output can take years to respond to higher prices.
items.answer: Opening a new mine requires exploration, permits, large investment and construction; capacity is fixed in the short run, so supply is inelastic.

items.stem: When the price received by a solar-panel plant in Malaysia changed from $5 to $6.25, quantity supplied changed from 2,000 to 2,250 panels per week. Calculate the PES.
items.answer: PES = 0.5 (price inelastic)

items.stem: Noah writes: "If a factory is working at full capacity, its supply is perfectly elastic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: At full capacity, output cannot rise easily, so supply is inelastic in the short run.
items.markingKey: At full capacity, output cannot rise easily, so supply is inelastic in the short run. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline why the prices of primary commodities are more volatile than the prices of manufactured goods.
items.answer: Two diagrams. Commodity: steep (inelastic) demand and supply; a supply shift (e.g. bad harvest) causes a large price change. Manufactured good: flatter (elastic) supply; the same demand or supply shift causes a smaller price change and a larger quantity change.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Two diagrams. Commodity: steep (inelastic) demand and supply; a supply shift (e.g. bad harvest) causes a large price change. Manufactured good: flatter (elastic) supply; the same demand or supply shift causes a smaller price change and a larger quantity change. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: The PES for output from a bakery in Vienna is estimated at 2. If the price rises by 20% from $10, calculate the new quantity supplied (currently 5,000 loaves per day), and explain one reason why supply might have this elasticity.
items.answer: 7000 loaves; price elastic

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how the price elasticity of supply changes over time after an increase in demand.
items.answer: Diagram: three supply curves through the original equilibrium – vertical momentary supply, steeper short-run supply, flatter long-run supply. After demand shifts right, price rises most in the momentary period and least in the long run, while quantity rises most in the long run.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Firms should always hold large stocks so that their supply is price elastic."
items.answer: Holding stocks increases PES, but the optimal level balances responsiveness against storage and financing costs.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stocks allow firms to respond quickly to price rises and gain revenue; reduces the risk of shortages. Arguments against: storage costs, waste and obsolescence; ties up working capital; perishable goods cannot be stored. Supported judgement: Holding stocks increases PES, but the optimal level balances responsiveness against storage and financing costs.
